# Water pollution — causes, effects, and control

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Water pollution — causes** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Environmental Issues fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Water pollution — causes
### effects
### and control

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

Water pollution is any change in water quality that harms life or usefulness. The big concepts: **BOD** (biochemical oxygen demand — the oxygen microbes need to decompose the waste; high BOD = dirty water), **eutrophication** (nutrient enrichment → algal bloom → oxygen crash), and **biomagnification** (toxics like DDT and mercury climbing the food chain). Control runs through sewage treatment and watershed management.

## 3. Classified tables

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — from discharge to damage (study in this order)**

| Step | Concept | Key detail |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sources | Sewage, industrial effluent, farm runoff (N, P), thermal discharge |
| 2 | Point vs non-point sources | Pipe outlet vs field runoff across a whole watershed |
| 3 | BOD as the measuring stick | More organic waste → more microbial oxygen demand → lower dissolved O2 |
| 4 | Eutrophication sequence | N + P enrich → algal bloom → bloom dies → decomposition eats O2 → fish kill |
| 5 | Biomagnification | DDT/mercury concentration multiplies ~10× per trophic level — top predators worst hit |
| 6 | Control | Sewage treatment (primary/secondary/tertiary), effluent norms, watershed protection |

**Water pollutants and their signature effects**

| Pollutant | Source | Signature effect |
|---|---|---|
| Organic sewage | Homes, food industry | High BOD, oxygen depletion, foul smell |
| Nitrates and phosphates | Fertiliser runoff, detergents | Eutrophication and algal blooms |
| Mercury | Industry (Minamata) | Biomagnified nerve poison in fish and humans |
| DDT and pesticides | Agriculture | Biomagnification; thin eggshells in birds of prey |
| Thermal discharge | Power plants | Warm water holds less O2 — aquatic stress |
| Pathogens | Untreated sewage | Cholera, typhoid, jaundice outbreaks |

**Sewage treatment — the three stages**

| Stage | What it removes | How |
|---|---|---|
| Primary | Large solids and grit | Screening, grit chamber, sedimentation |
| Secondary (biological) | Dissolved organic matter — the BOD | Aeration tank with microbial floc (activated sludge) or trickling filter; floc settles as sludge, partly recycled |
| Tertiary / final | Nutrients, pathogens, residual solids | Chlorination/UV, chemical precipitation; sludge digested anaerobically → biogas |

## 5. Worked examples and applications

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example — reading a BOD test.** Sample A: BOD 5 mg/L, dissolved oxygen 8 mg/L. Sample B: BOD 300 mg/L, dissolved oxygen 2 mg/L. Sample B carries heavy organic pollution — microbes will strip the remaining oxygen, fish will suffocate, and anaerobic decay will produce foul H2S. Sample A is healthy water. BOD is the single most useful number in water quality: it measures pollution by measuring the microbes' own appetite.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Eutrophication chain: nutrient (N, P) enrichment → algal bloom → O2 depletion → fish death → anaerobic decay (foul smell) — the five-step causal chain is the answer.
Trick 2: BOD: oxygen needed by microbes to decompose organic matter — higher BOD = more pollution; clean water BOD < 5 ppm; sewage treatment uses BOD reduction as its goal.
Trick 3: Biomagnification: DDT 0.003 ppb water → 25 ppm fish-eating birds (10 million×) — the classic magnification numerical; also mercury (Minamata).
Trick 4: Sewage treatment: primary (physical, settling) → secondary (biological, activated sludge) → tertiary (chemical); Flocs = masses of bacteria in aeration tanks.
